props.title: Badge
props.description: A short label that names a state or a count. It is not interactive, so it wears only the resting state of a control recipe and deliberately skips the shared state machine — a label that changed colour under the pointer would read as something you can press. Pick the recipe with `variant`, pick the ramp it resolves against with `tint`.

props.title: Variant and tint
props.description: Every combination the two axes allow — three of the six recipes, the ones that read as a label rather than as a control — plus the one variant the badge owns. `raised` is paper fill and quiet ink, no ramp: the chip that sits on a grey card, where a `tinted` neutral would sink into the card and a `filled` one would shout. There is no `normal` or `plain` badge, because both would be text with padding around it.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Each size borrows the padding of the control size one step below it, and sets its label in the caption face, so a badge reads as a label rather than as a control that stopped working.

props.title: Where it lands
props.description: The trailing cell of a table, the trailing slot of a preference row, the count on a navigation row. In all three it annotates something the row already names, which is why it stays small and never carries the only copy that matters. A leading dot needs no prop: the badge is an inline flex row and the glyph inherits its content colour.

props.title: Button
props.description: The six control recipes, each on any ramp. Hover, press, and disabled are not written here at all — `data-control` puts the recipe's own states on the element, so a button's stylesheet is the box and nothing else.

props.title: Variants
props.description: `normal` is the neutral control on the paper, edged by a hairline; `recessed` is the same control one step into the paper, the workaday grey chip a toolbar or a footer is full of, and the default. `filled` is the one action a view points at; `outlined` its drawn twin; `tinted` a quiet accent chip; `plain` looks like text at rest but keeps the box, because its recipe washes on hover.

props.title: Tints
props.description: Hover any of these: the hover and press states come from the same recipe, so a danger button darkens the way a primary one does. Nothing below sets a colour — each row is one variant read against six ramps. `recessed` and `normal` are absent on purpose: they are the neutral controls, reading the theme's surface and ink roles rather than a ramp, so `tint` leaves them untouched.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Button keeps no per-size block at all: the `[data-size]` profile carries the height, the padding, the radius and the type face, and the stylesheet reads them once.

props.title: Content
props.description: An icon is a child rather than a prop, so it costs the component no API and takes the button's own colour through `currentColor`. A shortcut is the one trailing slot, set in the button's colour at a lowered opacity — a key cap inside a button would read as a second control. There is no `loading` prop either: work in flight is a spinner in the label and `disabled` on the button.

props.title: In a row
props.description: Where more than one button sits together, the row is an ActionBar so the gap comes from the control scale. The confirming action goes last and is the only filled one: two filled buttons side by side ask the reader to choose which is the default.

props.title: Callout
props.description: A tinted notice that sits in the flow of a pane, above the thing it is about. That is the line between this and a Toast: a toast reports something that already happened somewhere else, a callout qualifies what you are looking at. The token graph gives it two type roles — a title and a description — so it is built for both, and drops the title when a one-line notice is all that is needed.

props.title: Tints
props.description: A callout always wears the tinted treatment; anything louder would be a dialog, not a callout. So the ramp is the only colour axis, and it is the whole message: `danger` is a failure, `warning` a caveat, `info` a fact worth knowing.

props.title: Card
props.description: The filled or bordered box the panels in a layout are built from. It is a container rather than a control, so its padding is uniform and comes off the spacing scale instead of the control scale, and it stays out of the shared state machine — a panel that washed under the pointer would read as something you can press.

props.title: Variants
props.description: Only `tinted` reads the tint; the rest resolve against the neutral surface and border roles. `raised` is a panel on the canvas, `sunken` a well inside one, `outlined` a boundary with no fill of its own.

children: Padding, gap, and radius all come from the size.

props.title: Tints
props.description: The tinted variant across every ramp: a 50 fill under a 200 border. The other three ignore `tint` entirely, so setting it on them is harmless and does nothing.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Padding, the gap between children, and the radius step together. Each step is a spacing token and a radius token, not a control profile — a card holds content rather than sitting in a row of controls.

props.title: What goes in one
props.description: A card is a flex column with the gap already set, so a heading row, a body, and a footer need no spacing of their own — only the row that has to spread its children apart. `sunken` is the recessed variant, for a region that holds something rather than being something.

props.title: Divider
props.description: A one-pixel rule. It carries no component tokens of its own: a separator is entirely described by a border colour and the hairline step of the spacing scale, and inventing `divider-*` aliases for those would only add a layer to read through.

props.title: Tones
props.description: The two border roles. `muted` is the lighter of the pair, for a rule inside a filled surface where the default would cut too hard; `default` is what separates one region from another.

props.title: Vertical
props.description: Stretches to its flex parent, so a toolbar row sizes it without a height being passed in. That is the whole reason it is a div rather than an `<hr>`: a rule that has to be told how tall it is will be told wrong somewhere.

props.title: In a container
props.description: A card already sets the gap between its children, so a divider adds only the line — it does not need margins, and giving it any would double the space the card had decided on.

props.title: EmptyState
props.description: What a pane shows before it has content: one muted line and at most one action. The surrounding chrome already names the pane, so there is no heading, no explainer copy, and no illustration. It centres in whatever it is given, so it needs no height of its own.

props.title: With and without an action
props.description: The action row takes the control gap rather than the block gap, because it holds controls. One action is the norm; two is the most it should ever carry, and only when neither is obviously the way out.

props.description: An empty pane and an empty result are different states and read differently: one says nothing has been added, the other says a filter matched nothing. Copy is the only thing carrying that difference, so it has to be exact.

props.title: IconButton
props.description: A square button with no label of its own, so `label` is required and doubles as the native tooltip. It reads the same control recipes as Button, plus a pressed state for a toggle that stays down. It defaults to `plain` on the neutral ramp: a toolbar of these should read as chrome, not as a row of accented actions.

props.title: Variants
props.description: The same five recipes a Button wears. `plain` is the default because most icon buttons are chrome; `filled` is for the one that leads — a compose, an add.

props.title: It does not latch
props.description: A glyph button that stays down is a `Toggle`, which is square at this same control height when its label is a lone glyph — so a latching glyph and a plain one sit in one toolbar without a seam. Keeping an on-state here as well would be a second drawing for one state, and the system draws a selection one way: a tinted wash and a heavier label.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: The button is square at the shared control height, so it lines up with the labelled buttons and the fields beside it. Size the glyph a couple of steps under the box — a glyph filling its button reads as a full stop.

props.title: Tints
props.description: Neutral by default, which is what a toolbar wants. Tint the one that carries a consequence — the delete — and leave the rest alone, or the row goes back to saying nothing.

props.title: KeyCap
props.description: One key, drawn three ways. It reads the theme's ink and surface roles directly and takes no tint — a key looks like a key whatever is around it. A cap says what the key *is*; where the key can be changed, that is a ShortcutRecorder instead.

props.title: Variants
props.description: `hint` — the default — is bare faint text in the display cut: the `⌘F` beside an empty search field, the `⌥2` in a card's corner, an aside the eye may skip. `strong` is the same a step darker, for a hint that has to survive on a busy row. `key` alone draws the cap — a recessed, chip-cornered fill with no border, since a key is pressed *into* the surface rather than raised off it — and is what a settings page lists shortcuts in.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Colours are shared across the three; only the type steps, and only at the top — `small` and `medium` set the same face, `large` goes one up. Pick the size from what the key sits beside: `small` next to body text, `medium` in a row of controls.

props.title: Chords
props.description: A chord is several caps composed by the caller, which keeps the separator the caller's decision: macOS sets its modifiers flush, a cross-platform app usually wants a `+` between them. A hint sets the whole chord in one cap — `⌘⇧K` is one glyph run, not three — and the cap sits on the text baseline it is set in, so a sentence naming a shortcut does not gain a line of leading.

props.title: Link
props.description: Text that goes somewhere. It is the one interactive thing in this package that is genuinely inline, which is why it exists beside Button variant='plain' rather than inside it: a button keeps its box at every variant, and a box is what a link in a sentence must not have. It takes the shared state machine for its colour — the plain recipe, a grade darker on hover — and none of its geometry.

props.title: Underline
props.description: `hover` is the default, because a paragraph with a rule under every link reads as struck through. `always` is for a link that has to be findable without a pointer — a list of references, a footer. `none` is for one whose surroundings already say it is a link: a breadcrumb, a row that is entirely a target.

props.title: External
props.description: Sets the target and the rel that keeps the opener out of the new page's reach, and draws the arrow that says so before the reader commits. The arrow is inline, so it wraps with the last word rather than stranding itself on a line of its own.

props.title: Tints
props.description: A link is accent text, so it reads the plain recipe's content grade off whichever ramp it is tinted with. Danger is the one worth reaching for — a link that deletes something.

props.title: OptionCard
props.description: The shape a small set of mutually exclusive choices takes when each needs a line of explanation and a radio row would not carry it. Wrap a set in a radiogroup. The description is optional, and a set that does not need one is really a SegmentedControl.

props.title: Picking one
props.description: Selection is the tinted recipe with the outlined recipe's border on top: the fill says which one is chosen, and the border makes it survive a glance across its neighbours. An option that cannot be picked stays in the row rather than being dropped, so the set keeps its shape and the reason can be written into the description.

props.title: OtpField
props.description: The one-time code a reader is copying out of a message. It is a run of cells rather than a single field because that is what makes it fast: Base UI moves the caret between them, takes a paste of the whole code into all of them at once, hands the browser the autofill hint that pulls the code out of an SMS, and can submit the form the moment the last cell fills.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Each cell is the text controls' box at one character wide, so a code sits on the same rhythm as the fields around it — a code entered in a box of its own design would be the only control on the page that was. The mono face and tabular figures keep the digits on one width.

props.title: Grouping
props.description: `groupAfter` breaks the run where a printed code breaks — three and three is how a six-digit code is read aloud. It is a step of air rather than a rule, because a rule would read as two fields.

props.title: Masked and disabled
props.description: `mask` is for a code that is a secret rather than a one-time token — a PIN. A filled cell lifts to the paper and keeps it, so the run says how far through the code the reader is without the caret having to be the only thing that does.

props.title: PillTabs
props.description: Free-standing filter pills. Unlike a segmented control there is no track holding them together, so each pill needs its own fill to be a target at all — which also means they can wrap, and a filter row usually has to. That is the reason to reach for them over a segmented control: a filter row grows with the data.

props.title: Filtering
props.description: A count rides inside the pill, dimmed against the label it follows rather than set beside it as a badge — a badge would be a second thing to read, and the number here is an attribute of the filter rather than a state of its own. A filter with nothing behind it stays in the row rather than disappearing, so the set does not reflow every time a permission changes.

props.title: Tints
props.description: The selected pill is the filled recipe, so the ramp is what picks it out. A filter row keeps one tint: the colour means “this one is on”, and varying it per pill would make it mean something about the pill.

props.title: Wrapping
props.description: Nine of them in a narrow column. A track that had to hold this many segments would run off the pane.

props.label: Balanced — a second pass on low scores

props.title: SearchField
props.description: Inline search for a list or a table. The box belongs to the wrapper rather than the input, because the glyph and the trailing slot sit inside it — which is also why the focus ring comes from `:focus-within`. It holds no results of its own, so the same component narrows a table, a rail, or a menu without knowing which.

props.title: The trailing slot
props.description: A hint sits there while the field is empty and gives way to the clear button once there is something to clear, so the two never compete for the same corner. Type something and press Escape: it clears first, and only dismisses once the field is already empty, so a stray press never closes a search mid-way.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: The glyph and the trailing slot hold their distance from the edges at every size, so the text starts and ends on the same inset a plain TextField's does.

props.title: Tints
props.description: The tint reaches the focus ring and the focused border. Focus each of these — nothing else about the field changes, because a search box is chrome and should not be carrying a colour of its own at rest.

props.title: SectionLabel
props.description: The micro-heading that organises a pane. Sentence case, no uppercasing and no added tracking — one size covers sidebars, rails, and pane headings, so tone is the only axis worth varying. `SidebarGroupLabel` and `PreferenceSection` both render one for you; this is what those are made of.

props.title: Tints
props.description: Untinted it takes the muted content colour, which is what a heading almost always wants. A tint moves it onto a ramp, for a heading that has to carry a state with it — a section reporting a failure, a group flagged for review.

props.title: Over a panel
props.description: It names what the numbers below it are. The card already sets the gap, so the label needs no margin — which is the reason it is a span rather than a heading element with a browser margin to undo.

props.title: Skeleton
props.description: The shape of something that has not arrived. A Spinner says the app is busy; a skeleton says what is coming and where it will be — which is why it belongs on the first load of a view whose layout is already known, and a spinner belongs on an action whose result is not. Drawing one for content that then lands somewhere else is worse than drawing nothing.

props.title: Shapes
props.description: `text` is a bar on the line box of the type it stands in for, so it needs no height. `circle` is an avatar or a glyph and squares itself from its width alone. `rect` is everything with a box of its own — a thumbnail, a chart, a card.

props.title: Lines
props.description: A paragraph's worth of bars, with the last one short. The ragged edge is most of what makes a block of bars legible as text at all — a full-width final line reads as a table.

props.title: Materials
props.description: The fill is surface-sunken — the same dead step a disabled control flattens to, which is exactly what a skeleton is. The sweep over it is surface-subtle, the ink wash the whole system already hovers with, so the highlight moves by the same amount on paper, on a card and on a dark canvas without a per-theme value. Unlike the spinner it takes no reduced-motion exception: a still spinner reads as a hung app, where a still skeleton still says everything it has to say.

props.title: StepList
props.description: A pipeline, one line per stage. The marker carries the status — a check when a stage is finished, the spinner while it runs, an empty ring before it starts — so the label never has to say it twice. Each is a different marker rather than a different colour of the same one, which is what lets the column be read at a glance and still work in monochrome. The list holds no state: the host passes each stage its status.

props.title: In flight
props.description: A finished step is success wherever the list is tinted: it is the one fixed meaning in the column, not a variation on the accent. The trailing detail — a count, a duration, a size — is pushed to the far edge and set back, so a column of them lines up without competing with the labels.

props.title: Finished
props.description: Every stage done, so nothing in the column is asking for attention. This is the state a list should be able to end in without changing shape — no summary row appearing, no markers moving.

props.title: Tints
props.description: The tint reaches the active step — its spinner and its label. A finished step stays on the success ramp whatever the list is tinted with, because “done” is a fixed meaning rather than an accent.

props.title: Tag
props.description: A Badge you can act on. The two are one drawing and two components rather than one component with an `interactive` prop, because the difference is not cosmetic: a badge reads its recipes at rest and stays out of the shared state machine, since a label that moves under the pointer reads as something you can press. A tag is something you can press — and taking the state machine is the whole reason it exists.

props.title: Beside a Badge
props.description: They share the capsule — the same box at the same three densities, written once in badge.css — and nothing else. A tag that is neither selectable nor removable should be a Badge.

props.title: Selected
props.description: Drawn twice over: the tinted fill the component swaps the variant to, and the tint's edge. One alone is not enough — a tinted tag that was already tinted would look untouched, and an edge alone is a pixel to spot in a row of forty.

props.title: Dismissing
props.description: The dismiss button is its own control rather than a second job for the label: a chip that removes itself when clicked has no way to be selected, and one that does both from the same target removes things by accident. It is faint at rest and only resolves under the pointer — an ✕ at full strength on every chip turns a list of tags into a list of buttons.

props.title: Sizes and variants
props.description: Both are the Badge's, because the capsule is the Badge's. What is added is the resting, hover, pressed and disabled states the recipes already carry.

props.title: ToggleGroup
props.description: Several toggles that belong together, joined into one control. Joined rather than merely adjacent: the corners are rounded at the ends of the run only and the shared edges collapse to one, which is what says the group is one thing with several states rather than three buttons that happen to touch.

props.title: Beside a SegmentedControl
props.description: This is where the two part company. A segmented control is a choice between its segments and always has exactly one; a toggle group can have several on at once, or none. Drawing a mandatory single choice with this one would let the reader clear a choice that cannot be cleared.

props.title: One tab stop
props.description: Base UI owns the part that is easy to get wrong: the group is a single tab stop and the arrow keys move inside it, which is what keeps a toolbar of twelve toggles from being twelve stops on the way to the document.

props.title: Words
props.description: Nothing about the group is glyph-only. A run of labelled toggles is what a filter bar wants, and the joined edges are what say the three answers are about one question.
